findings.claim: Six lessons describe the exam as a two-part question with a part (a) extract task and a part (b) wider-text task, and L8 puts the split at 20 marks + 20 marks with 20 minutes on each part.
findings.truth: Section A of the second component is ONE source-based question worth 40 marks, with an extract printed on the paper. There is no (a)/(b) split. The whole component is 2 hours 30 minutes for three 40-mark sections, so the drama question is worth about 50 minutes.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md s.2.2 Component 2 Section A (40 marks, 'through a source based response')

findings.claim: AO4 is repeatedly defined as context: 'AO4 (context)' in L1's glossary and content, 'AO4 (Priestley's socialist context)' in L2, 'a link to context (AO4)' in L4/L7/L8, and L8 tells students to embed AO4 context in every paragraph. Three top-band mark-scheme descriptors also reward context ('Context: 1945 election', 'Context: Priestley's socialism and BBC broadcasts', 'Priestley's socialism as context').
findings.truth: Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 only. AO4 in this specification is technical accuracy (spelling, punctuation, grammar), and AO3 (context) is NOT assessed on this question. Telling students context earns marks here is mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md s.2.2 Component 2 Section A ('Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4'; Section B, which does assess context, is the 19th-century prose question and assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3)

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions are labelled '20 marks — Extract Analysis' or '20 marks — Wider Text Response', tagged [20] in the question text, and marked with a 17-20 / 13-16 / 9-12 / 5-8 / 1-4 band ladder.
findings.truth: The question is a single 40-mark source-based response. Relabelled to '40 marks — Source-Based Response' with the house ladder 33-40 / 25-32 / 17-24 / 9-16 / 1-8, matching the sibling Eduqas post-1914 units.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md s.2.2 Component 2 Section A

findings.claim: 'Eduqas' is named in student-facing text eleven times (L1 content + glossary + exam tip, L2 key fact + exam tip, L3 exam tip, L4 exam tip, L5 exam tip, L6 content x2 + exam tip, L8 description + knowledge check + flashcard).
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas lessons never name the board in student-facing text. Reworded to 'the exam', 'your drama question', neutral phrasing.
findings.evidence: house rule (feedback_eduqas_wjec_neutral_phrasing)

findings.claim: 'These girls aren't cheap labour - they're people' is attributed to the Inspector nine times (L2 key fact + revision tip + knowledge check 3 + flashcard 2 + practice Q2; L7 content n6 + knowledge check 5 stem + flashcard 5 + practice Q2 and Q6).
findings.truth: The line is SHEILA's, in Act 1. It is her answer to the Inspector, who has just said that factories 'wouldn't know where to look for cheap labour. Ask your father.' Marking it as the Inspector's would lose a student credit for knowledge of the text.
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): 'Inspector: ... the factories and warehouses wouldn't know where to look for cheap labour. Ask your father. / Sheila: But these girls aren't cheap labour - they're people.'

findings.claim: Mrs Birling is said to remain 'rather agitated but quite determined' after the Inspector's speech (L3 content + flashcard, L5 content + flashcard + practice Q2, L8 content).
findings.truth: No such stage direction exists. The play gives Mrs Birling '(agitated now)' and '(rather agitated now)' in Act 2 and '(agitated)' when Eric is exposed; 'looking rather agitated' belongs to Birling. Her real unrepentant lines are 'Unlike the other three, I did nothing I'm ashamed of' (Act 2) and 'I was the only one of you who didn't give in to him' (Act 3).
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): no occurrence of 'quite determined' anywhere in the play

findings.claim: L7 twice quotes the Inspector speaking of Eva's 'her feelings and her hopes'.
findings.truth: That phrase is not in the play. The final speech has 'their hopes and fears, their suffering and chance of happiness'. Replaced with the real wording.
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): no occurrence of 'feelings and her hopes'

findings.claim: L3 says Mrs Birling 'describes Eva's appeal as giving “a lot of silly, nonsensical things”'.
findings.truth: Fabricated. Mrs Birling says Eva 'was giving herself ridiculous airs. She was claiming elaborate fine feelings and scruples that were simply absurd in a girl in her position.' ('not satisfied' is real - 'I wasn't satisfied with the girl's claim'.)
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): no occurrence of 'nonsensical'

findings.claim: 'In 1945, Priestley helped found the Common Wealth Party.'
findings.truth: The Common Wealth Party was founded on 26 July 1942, from the 1941 Committee and Forward March; Priestley was its first chair and stepped down within months. 1945 is the year of the Labour landslide, which the sentence goes on to mention.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Wealth_Party

findings.claim: 'Public men have responsibilities as well as privileges' is said to be 'spoken by the Inspector in Act 1' (L1), and dated '(Act 1)' in a L7 mark scheme.
findings.truth: The line is in Act 2: 'Inspector: (massively) Public men, Mr Birling, have responsibilities as well as privileges.'
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): the line falls between the Act 2 opening and 'END OF ACT TWO'

findings.claim: L3: 'Throughout Act 2, Sheila becomes increasingly perceptive. She warns Gerald: “You fool - he knows. Of course he knows.”'
findings.truth: That warning is the closing speech of Act 1, immediately before the Inspector reappears and the curtain falls. L6 already places the Gerald cliffhanger at the end of Act 1, so the unit contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): 'Sheila: (laughs rather hysterically) why - you fool - he knows...' then 'END OF ACT ONE'

findings.claim: L2: 'After the women leave the dining room ... Birling delivers his infamous speech to Gerald and Eric. He dismisses the threat of war ... and praises the Titanic as unsinkable.'
findings.truth: Wrong order. The Titanic and war speech is delivered at the table with Mrs Birling and Sheila present (Mrs Birling 'shows signs of interrupting'). Only after they withdraw does Birling give the 'cranks' and 'mind his own business' speech that the doorbell cuts off.
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): the Titanic speech precedes 'she and Sheila and Eric go out'

findings.claim: Flashcard 1 asks 'Which Birling line dismissively labels socialists “cranks”?' but the answer given is 'A man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own.'
findings.truth: Question and answer do not match; the answer contains no reference to cranks. The question has been rewritten to fit the answer that is on the card.
findings.evidence: internal mismatch

findings.claim: Flashcard 2 asks 'Which Eric line captures the social scale of Birling's sin?' with the answer 'I was in that state when a chap easily turns nasty.'
findings.truth: Question and answer do not match; the line is Eric admitting he was drunk and aggressive on the night he forced himself on Eva. Question rewritten to fit.
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): Eric, Act 3

findings.claim: L6 practice Q4 mark scheme quotes 'Birling is “ashen” faced' at the end of the play.
findings.truth: No such word appears. The stage direction is: 'He puts the telephone down slowly and looks in a panic-stricken fashion at the others.'
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): final page of Act 3

findings.claim: L3 quotes Gerald as saying 'She was pretty and warm-hearted - and intensely grateful.'
findings.truth: The line is 'She was young and pretty and warm-hearted - and intensely grateful.'
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): Gerald, Act 2

findings.claim: 'Gross' is applied to Eva herself: 'Eva's manner seemed “gross”' (L3 content, knowledge check 2 option, flashcard 8) and 'Gross - adjective dehumanises Eva' (L8 practice Q3).
findings.truth: Mrs Birling's word is about the use of the name, not the girl: 'I think it was simply a piece of gross impertinence - quite deliberate.' She separately says 'I didn't like her manner.' A student who writes that Mrs Birling calls Eva gross has misread the line.
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): Mrs Birling, Act 2

findings.claim: L8: 'Birling sees her as “cheap labour”' and a mark scheme item 'Birling: “cheap labour.”'
findings.truth: The phrase is the Inspector's, about factories in general, and Sheila's in reply. Birling never says it. Reworded so no quotation is attributed to Birling.
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition)

findings.claim: L5 flashcard 10: 'Birling bought his knighthood's prospect.'
findings.truth: Birling has not bought or received a knighthood; he says there is 'a very good chance of a knighthood' if there is no scandal.
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition): Birling, Act 1

findings.claim: L4 quotes the Inspector's final speech with 'all intertwined with our lives, with what we think and say and do' and a comma before 'and chance of happiness'.
findings.truth: Most printed texts read 'all intertwined with our lives, and what we think and say and do', with no comma after 'suffering'. Sources disagree on this preposition (school transcripts and revision sites split between 'and what' and 'with what'), so this is recorded rather than edited. If Tom wants it changed, the correction is one word.
findings.evidence: conflicting sources; full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition) reads 'and what'

findings.claim: L2 (the Act 1 lesson) presents Sheila's 'I know I'm to blame - and I'm desperately sorry' as her reaction inside the Milwards confession.
findings.truth: The Milwards confession and the '(miserably) So I'm really responsible?' stage direction are Act 1, but that quotation is spoken in Act 2. The lesson makes no explicit act claim about the line, so nothing is edited; worth knowing if the passage is ever rewritten.
findings.evidence: full play text (Ormiston Horizon Academy transcript of the Heinemann edition)

findings.claim: L4 flashcard 5 calls the 'fire and blood and anguish' warning a prediction of 'divine punishment'.
findings.truth: The speech has a biblical register, but the play frames the warning as the consequence of human failure, not a judgement from God. Defensible as an interpretation, so left alone.
findings.evidence: interpretive

summary: Every lesson taught another board's two-part 20 + 20 format and defined AO4 as context, so all 48 practice questions and six exam tips were relabelled to the single 40-mark source-based question that assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 (written accuracy). Three quotations were misattributed or invented: Sheila's 'these girls aren't cheap labour' was given to the Inspector nine times, Mrs Birling was given a stage direction ('rather agitated but quite determined') that does not exist, and the Inspector was given a line ('her feelings and her hopes') that does not exist.
